input.message:
Good work, and finding 1 is the important one. A verification gate that a hostile change can talk into VERIFIED by default is not acceptable, so two changes before I review. Same worktree, same constraints as before (allowed files only, no commit or push, foreground only, throwaway HOME, three consecutive passing runs of every new or changed test file, tsc clean, generators' --check, mutation checks restored).

## 1. Confinement becomes the default
- `nexus verify` with no `--sandbox` option behaves as `--sandbox auto`: use an available engine (keep the engine preference `run` uses for auto).
- If NO engine is usable and the operator did not explicitly choose to run unconfined, the verdict is BLOCKED / `SANDBOX_UNAVAILABLE` (exit 3), nothing is run, and the message says how to proceed: install an engine, or pass `--sandbox none` for a change you trust.
- `--sandbox none` is the explicit opt-out. It runs as today, MAY reach VERIFIED, and the result says so every time: the text output carries a line such as `unconfined: the verifier ran with your privileges; a hostile change could have forged this result` and the document records `sandbox: {requested: "none", engine: null, ...}`. Do not cap the verdict in this mode (the operator chose it), but make the statement impossible to miss, and assert its exact text in a test.
- The action (`action/verify/action.yml`): default the `sandbox` input to `auto`, document `none` as the opt-out for trusted branches, and keep the example on an explicit engine. Update `docs/VERIFY_IN_CI.md` and the manual: the default, what BLOCKED/SANDBOX_UNAVAILABLE means, and that VERIFIED from an unconfined run is only as trustworthy as the change.
- Existing tests: the fixture helper should pass `sandbox: "none"` explicitly by default so the existing suites keep their speed and meaning, and say so in a comment; add focused tests for the new default (engine available → sandboxed and recorded; no engine → BLOCKED with nothing run; explicit none → runs, with the unconfined line and record). The "no engine" case must be testable without uninstalling anything: check how you already inject engine availability for the `SANDBOX_UNAVAILABLE` composition test and reuse it.
- This changes behaviour of slices 1 and 2, which are merged on the release branch but in no release. Say so in the report so I can put it in the PR.

## 2. Defence in depth for the unconfined mode: materialise the judging copy before untrusted code runs, and check it afterwards
Today the pristine copy is written after the head run from the scratch index and object directory, which the head's own test could rewrite. Change the order and add a check, entirely inside `verify.ts`:
- Compute and hold IN MEMORY, before any untrusted process starts, the identity of each tree the verdict depends on (the base and head tree ids, and for the working-tree mode the tree id produced from the caller's files).
- Materialise the pristine copy BEFORE the head verifier runs.
- After all untrusted processes have ended, and before anything is judged, re-derive the identity of the pristine copy's contents with fresh scratch state created after the runs (a new index and a new object directory with unpredictable names, never the ones that existed during the runs) and compare it with the in-memory tree id. Do the same for any other on-disk state you then read to judge (the base copy the guard policy is read from, if it is read after a run: prefer reading everything you can BEFORE the first untrusted process).
- A mismatch, or any failure to complete the check, is a new reason (for example `SCRATCH_TAMPERED`): BLOCKED, exit 3, with a detail that names which copy differed. Never VERIFIED, never a silent re-materialisation.
- Be honest in code comments and docs about what this does and does not achieve: it defeats the exploit you wrote and its obvious variants, it does not make an unconfined run safe (a process that outlives the run, or one that tampers between the check and the read, can still interfere; say which windows remain). The manual's statement for `--sandbox none` stays as strong as in point 1.
- Tests: your finding-1 exploit, run with `--sandbox none`, must now end BLOCKED / `SCRATCH_TAMPERED` (assert the reason and that the verdict is not VERIFIED); a variant that edits the pristine copy directly; a variant that edits the base copy; and a clean run still reaches VERIFIED with `--sandbox none`. Keep the sandboxed version of the exploit test. Mutation: remove the post-run comparison and confirm the exploit test fails with VERIFIED.
- If a new reason is added, the schema changes again: regenerate, and since your earlier ledger entry for this slice is NOT yet published, UPDATE that same appended entry's hash and note rather than adding a third entry (the first, published entry stays untouched).

## 3. Small items
- The example workflow pins `mikeholownych/nexus-code/action/verify@v1.3.0`, a tag that does not exist yet. Keep it (it is what users will write after the release) but add a comment in the example and in `docs/VERIFY_IN_CI.md` that the tag exists from v1.3.0, and make the action test not depend on the tag existing.
- The UTF-8 refusal also refuses a legitimate name containing U+FFFD: leave it, state it in the manual's limits.
- Finding 7 (my brief's wording): no change needed; keep the test.

Report: what changed since your last report only; the exact unconfined line; which windows remain open in unconfined mode after change 2; test commands with pass/fail/skip counts and durations for every new or changed file plus `verify_command`, `verify_typecheck_guard`, `verify_schema`; the mutation result; schema and ledger state; anything you could not do. ## 2. Design

### Format (section 3 of your brief)

No TOML parser exists anywhere:
- `cli/package.json` runtime dependencies are `commander`, `dotenv`, `ora`, `picocolors`.
- `core/Cargo.toml` has `serde` and `serde_json` only.
- Node 22/24 has no TOML module.
- `security.ts:213-223` is a section-header regex, not a parser.

**Recommended default: a strict hand-written TOML subset, keeping D16's `.toml` paths.**

| | TOML subset | JSON |
|---|---|---|
| Matches D16 text | yes | needs a plan amendment (PLAN.md is claimed) |
| Comments for admins | yes | no |
| Duplicate keys | rejected by our parser | `JSON.parse` silently takes the last one, so `{"strict":true,"strict":false}` yields false |
| Parser risk | about 200 lines to own and test | none |
| User expectation | people will write full TOML and be rejected | none |

The duplicate-key problem means JSON would need a custom scanner too, so the parser cost is not avoided by choosing JSON. The user-expectation cost is mitigated by line-numbered errors and `nexus policy check <file>`.

**Grammar accepted:**
- UTF-8, LF or CRLF, no BOM, no control characters except tab.
- Blank lines; `#` comments (full-line or trailing).
- Root `key = value` lines before any table.
- `[table]` headers, single level.
- Keys and table names match `[a-z][a-z0-9_]*`.
- Values: a basic string `"…"` on one line with only the `\"` and `\\` escapes; `true` / `false`; a non-negative decimal integer; an array of basic strings (may span lines, trailing comma and comments allowed).

**Rejected, each with `line N`:**
- Literal or multi-line strings, any other escape.
- Floats, signs, hex, underscores, dates.
- Inline tables, dotted or quoted keys, `[[…]]`, nested or mixed arrays.
- Duplicate key, duplicate table.
- Anything after a value except a comment.
- Strings over 1024 characters, arrays over 500 items, files over 64 KiB.

**Shape and size:** output is `{root, tables}` with a line number per key; the parser is schema-agnostic and the validator rejects unknown tables and keys. About 180-220 lines.

**Parser tests:**
- About 25 accepted documents.
- About 60 rejected documents, asserting line and message.
- Render-then-parse round trip for generated documents.
- A mutation loop asserting only `PolicyParseError` is ever thrown.

### Schema

One normalized `PolicyDocument` type covers all tiers. The two managed tiers are TOML. The project tier stays `.nexus-security.json`, mapped by an adapter.

**Recommendation on restrict-only: encode it in both the types and the merge.** `PolicyDocument` has no field that can express a grant, and the merge is a lattice meet proven by a generated table.

| Key | Type | Merge | Enforces |
|---|---|---|---|
| `schema_version` | int, required in managed tiers | n/a | version rule in section 5 |
| `approval.strict` | bool | OR | shorthand for the next three |
| `approval.disable_auto` | bool | OR | mode `auto` from any source |
| `approval.disable_yes` | bool | OR | `-y/--yes`, including `verify --yes` |
| `approval.disable_full_access` | bool | OR | any `fullAccess` source |
| `approval.require_human` | array of `exec`, `write_workspace`, `egress` | union | always ask, even under full access |
| `verification.mode` | `approve` or `block` only | max | a floor; `off` and `record` are type errors |
| `verification.protected` | globs | union | extra protected paths |
| `commands.forbid`, `commands.prompt` | prefix strings such as `"git push"` | union | CS-9 rules; no `allow` key exists |
| `commands.disable_allow_rules` | bool | OR | drops the user's `allow` rules |
| `paths.protected` | patterns | union | |
| `egress.inspector` | `record` or `block` | max | floor over `NEXUS_EGRESS_POLICY` |
| `egress.allowed_domains` | allowlist | intersection | |
| `egress.secret_destinations` | allowlist | intersection | caps `allowDestinations` |
| `sandbox.required` | bool | OR | |
| `sandbox.forbid_network` | bool | OR | |
| `mcp.allow` | allowlist: `name`, `command:/abs/path`, `url:https://origin` | intersection | |
| `mcp.disable_workspace` | bool | OR | |
| `plugins.allow` | allowlist: `sha256:<hex>`, `file:/abs/path` | intersection | |
| `plugins.disable_workspace` | bool | OR | |
| `workspace.disable_env_trust` | bool | OR | ignores `NEXUS_TRUST_WORKSPACE` |

- **Allowlists:** absent means unrestricted; present (even empty) means only the listed items; absent is the identity for intersection.
- **Legacy project relaxations** (`mode` `off`/`record`, `verificationPaths.allow`) live in a separate `ProjectRelaxations` type. They apply only when the workspace is trusted, integrity is MATCH, and no managed tier sets `verification.mode`.
- So a trusted project may relax a built-in default only where no managed tier has spoken, exactly as today.

### Merge and attribution

- `mergePolicies(system?, user?, project?) → EffectivePolicy`, frozen.
- Because the merge is a meet, precedence cannot change the value; it decides attribution only.
- For a scalar, the deciding tier is the highest tier whose own value equals the effective value. Each list element carries the first tier that contributed it. Otherwise the source is `default`.
- `PolicySource = { tier: "system"|"user"|"project"|"operator-rules"|"default", file?, key, line? }`.
- One renderer, `describeSource`, produces for example `[policy: system /etc/nexus/policy.toml approval.strict]`.
- Every prompt and denial string appends it, including `[policy: default]`. That is how "the effective tier is printed beside every decision" is met.

### Modules

- `cli/src/core/managed_policy.ts`: pure types, validation, merge, clamp helpers, `describeSource`.
- `cli/src/core/managed_policy_toml.ts`: the parser.
- `cli/src/core/managed_policy_load.ts`: file-system reads with every input explicit — `loadManagedPolicy({ systemPath, systemOwnerUid, userPath, userUid, workspace, trust, fs })`.
- One composition function binds the constants and memoizes once per process.
- Until `types.ts` and `agent.ts` are free, consumers take an optional `policy` parameter that defaults to the memo (the same style as module state at `config.ts:33-34`). Afterwards it is threaded through `HarnessConfig.managedPolicy`.

### Fail-closed rules

Both managed tiers throw `ManagedPolicyError { tier, file, code, line? }`.

| Condition | System tier | User tier |
|---|---|---|
| File absent | tier absent | tier absent |
| `/etc/nexus` exists but is not root-owned, or is group/world-writable, or is a symlink | refuse | n/a |
| Symlink (`lstat` or `ELOOP`) | refuse | refuse (same as `config.ts:641`) |
| Not a regular file (opened with `O_NONBLOCK`) | refuse | refuse |
| `EACCES`, `EIO`, any other error | refuse | refuse |
| Over 64 KiB | refuse | refuse |
| Owner | must be uid 0 | must be euid or 0 |
| Mode has `0o022` bits | refuse | refuse |
| `fstat` dev/ino differs from `lstat` | refuse | refuse |
| Invalid UTF-8, BOM, NUL | refuse | refuse |
| Syntax error, duplicate, unknown table or key, wrong type, bad enum | refuse | refuse |
| Empty file or missing `schema_version` | refuse | refuse |
| `schema_version` above supported | refuse | refuse |

**Exit code 2**, matching existing configuration failures (`index.ts:54-60, 122-127`). On `nexus run` this shares code 2 with `unverified` and `usage` (`run_contract.ts:72-73`). Stderr is two lines:

```
nexus: managed policy error (system tier): /etc/nexus/policy.toml: line 7: unknown key 'approval.disable_yess'.
Nexus will not start without this policy. Fix the file (root-owned; ask your administrator) and run `nexus doctor`. No setting or environment variable bypasses it.
```

The user-tier variant ends: `Fix it, or move it aside: mv ~/.config/nexus/policy.toml ~/.config/nexus/policy.toml.bad`.

**Recovery path:**
- `--version`, `--help`, `nexus doctor` and `nexus policy check` always run. Doctor follows the deferred-error pattern at `config.ts:109-113`.
- The system tier has no override of any kind.
- `doctor --fix` never touches policy files.

### Project integrity

- **Store:** `~/.config/nexus/policy_trust.json`, written with `writePrivateFile`, keyed by workspace real path, value `{sha256, approvedAt}`.
- **Order:** bounded no-follow read → SHA-256 → status → strict parse → split into the restrictive part and relaxations.
- **Statuses:** ABSENT, NEW, MATCH, MISMATCH, REMOVED.
- **The restrictive part always applies**, as it does today for untrusted workspaces.
- **Relaxations apply only on trusted and MATCH.**
- **Interactive NEW or MISMATCH with relaxations:** ask, show the relaxations, record on yes.
- **Headless:** never ask. Drop the relaxations, apply the restrictive part, emit a notice, and record it. The run continues tighter, and an edit that needed the relaxation ends BLOCKED through the existing `needs_input` path (`dispatch_tool_call.ts:342-361`).
- **`NEXUS_TRUST_WORKSPACE=1`** counts as status `ENV_TRUSTED` for CI, unless `workspace.disable_env_trust` is set.
- **A project parse error stays non-fatal** but becomes loud: built-in defaults, no relaxations, a notice, and a doctor warning.

### GV-5 refusals

All exit 2 at launch.

| Trigger | Message |
|---|---|
| `--yes` under `disable_yes` or `strict` | `nexus: --yes is disabled by managed policy (system tier, /etc/nexus/policy.toml, approval.strict). Run without it; approvals will be asked.` |
| `--mode auto`, or `NEXUS_APPROVAL_MODE=auto` | `nexus: mode 'auto' (from --mode) is disabled by managed policy (<source>). Use --mode review or --mode read-only.` |
| `/mode auto`, the "always" answer, sidecar always-approve | not an exit: mode unchanged, the one call is approved, notice printed with the source |
| `--sandbox none` or no sandbox under `sandbox.required` | forced to `auto` plus `requireSandbox`; an explicit `none` is refused |
| `--sandbox-network` or `NEXUS_SANDBOX_NETWORK` under `forbid_network` | refused at launch |
| MCP server not in `mcp.allow` | not connected; `MCP server 'x' not started: not in mcp.allow (<source>)` |
| Plugin not in `plugins.allow` | not imported; same form |

**CS-9 agreement:**
- Managed `forbid` and `prompt` rules are evaluated by the same `decideCommand`, in a combined set.
- A managed `prompt` holds under full access. This changes `dispatch_tool_call.ts:448` for managed-sourced rules only.
- `CommandRuleDecision` gains an optional `source`.

## 5. Security analysis for G-3

| Attack | Rule that stops it |
|---|---|
| A lower tier loosens a higher one | No grant is expressible; the merge is a meet; relaxations are void where a managed tier speaks. |
| Deleting the user or project file | An absent tier is the identity, so the result is never below the system tier. Deleting the project file can only remove relaxations. |
| Deleting the system file | Needs root; an unsafe `/etc/nexus` directory fails closed. |
| A repository plants `policy.toml` | Only two fixed absolute paths are read as managed; nothing under the workspace or cwd. |
| Project file honoured before trust | Bytes are hashed before parsing; relaxations require trusted and MATCH. See the open decision in section 8. |
| Environment variables | No variable names a policy path. `NEXUS_TRUST_WORKSPACE`, `NEXUS_APPROVAL_MODE`, `NEXUS_SANDBOX_NETWORK` and `NEXUS_EGRESS_POLICY` are all clamped after the merge. |
| `HOME` or `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` redirected | Affects only the user tier, which the user owns anyway; the system path is absolute. |
| Symlink or swap race | `lstat`, `O_NOFOLLOW`, `fstat` dev/ino comparison, loaded once, frozen. |
| Malformed, truncated or duplicate key | Strict parser; an empty file is an error. |
| Newer file read by an older Nexus | Every key addition bumps `schema_version`; a reader accepts only its supported set and fails closed on a higher one. Rollout order: Nexus first, then policy. |
| Corrupt `command_rules.json` | Under any managed tier, a load failure drops `allow` rules only. |
| Model edits the policy files | Protected paths plus the `policy` verification class. |

**Residual risks to document:**
- An unsandboxed shell running as the user can edit the user tier and `policy_trust.json` for the next run. Only the system tier is tamper-resistant.
- An admitted in-process plugin can defeat any in-process control (PLAN.md:88), so `plugins.allow` with hashes is the real control.
- An `mcp.allow` entry by bare name is spoofable by whoever writes `mcp.json`; pin with `command:` or `url:`.

## 6. Acceptance tests

- **Precedence table (`managed_policy_merge.test.ts`).** Generated.

| Decision | Recommended default |

| Format | TOML subset at D16's paths |
| System path | The constant `/etc/nexus/policy.toml`, not configurable at build or run time |

## What managed policy will be
- **Three tiers, fixed precedence:** a system file an administrator owns (`/etc/nexus/policy.toml`), a user file, and the project's existing `.nexus-security.json`.
- **Restrict-only by construction.** The policy types have no field that can grant anything. Tiers combine by "most restrictive wins" for every key, so a lower tier can't loosen a higher one, and deleting a file can never drop below the system tier.
- **Fails closed.** A broken or tampered system or user file stops `nexus` with a message naming the file and line. Nothing bypasses the system tier. `--version`, `--help` and `nexus doctor` still run, so an operator isn't locked out of diagnosis.
- **Admin controls (GV-5)** are keys in the same file: a strict mode that refuses `--yes` and auto mode, a required sandbox, no network, and allowlists for MCP servers and plugins.

## Slice 1 is a pure library
It adds the parser, the schema, the merge, the hardened file loader and the project-file integrity check as new files only. It is not enforced yet, and the docs will say so at the top. Enforcement comes in later slices, some of which need files another lane currently holds.

## What the planning pass found in today's code
- **Project policy fails open.** A malformed `.nexus-security.json` silently falls back to defaults, dropping the project's own restrictions with no message. Slice 2 will make that loud.
- **Operator command rules fail open the same way** when they can't be loaded.
- **A "require a prompt" command rule is skipped under `--yes`.** A system-level rule must not be skippable that way.
- **Plugins can't be allow-listed by name.** A plugin's name is only known after its code has run, so the allowlist has to key on the file's hash.

## Decisions I took from the plan's defaults
- **File format:** a strict subset of TOML, at the paths the plan names. JSON looked simpler but silently accepts duplicate keys, so it would have needed a custom parser anyway.
- **System policy path:** a fixed constant, not changeable by any setting or environment variable.
- **User tier:** fails closed too, with a documented "move the file aside" recovery.

The full plan is at `/home/mike/nexus-wt/_plans/GV1_PLAN.md`.

## 3. Defects and weaknesses

### Correctness

1. **Stale buffers in other open files (verified).** `syncFile` updates only the queried file (354-394) and nothing is ever closed. Once file B has been opened by any LSP call, the server keeps B's old in-memory text after the agent edits B on disk. Diagnostics, hover and definition for A that depend on B are then computed against old B and reported as `ok`.
2. **A list cached before first open is returned as current.** A publish for a never-opened URI is stored (263-267). The first-open branch does not clear it (369-371), and `firstDiagnostics` returns it immediately (420-421). Whether servers publish package-wide before open (gopls, rust-analyzer) is my inference; the code path is verified.
3. **The tool timeout defeats the Rust settling design (verified constants).** The tool uses 5000 ms (`cli/src/tools.ts:1641`; 587). The post-edit window is 8000 ms (line 9; 411), so the loop always ends on the timeout and returns whatever is cached. `docs/LSP_REAL_SERVERS.md` records about 13-18 s for a first Rust call, so the first `lsp_diagnostics` on Rust is expected to return "published no diagnostics within 5000ms" (inferred from the documented timing).
4. **Position units are undefined.** There is no `positionEncodings` negotiation (154-164) and no conversion (446, 463). The schema says "character offset" (`capability_definitions/lsp.ts:29, 68`). A column counted in code points or bytes is wrong on any line with astral or non-ASCII text before the symbol. Diagnostic columns are UTF-16 units plus one (`cli/src/diagnostics.ts:233`).
5. **Definition output is inconsistent with its input.** It returns 0-based ranges and `file://` URIs (`cli/src/tools.ts:1631`), while inputs and diagnostics are 1-based workspace paths. The model must add one to chain calls, and nothing tells it so.
6. **URI identity.** The URI comes from the unresolved path (367, 398) and `rootPath` is not a real path (120). A server that canonicalises paths publishes under a different URI, the waiter never fires, and the result is "unavailable" (inferred). Exact-string keys are also sensitive to percent-encoding differences.
7. **Severity.** Hints are reported as "information" (258).
8. **Server requests.** `workspace/applyEdit` gets `null` rather than `{applied: false}`, and unknown methods get a success instead of MethodNotFound (321). The three methods you named are answered acceptably.
9. **Hover and definition have no readiness wait.** `syncFile` is followed immediately by the request (622-625, 645-648). The real-server tests need retries (docs, "Hover and definition" paragraph), so a first call in the product commonly returns "No hover info" or an empty list with `success: false`, which is indistinguishable from "no symbol here".

### Robustness

10. **Missing binary.** The `error` handler only clears a flag (132-134) and does not reject the pending `initialize`. A missing server therefore appears to cost the full 5 s on every call (inferred from Node's spawn behaviour; needs a characterising test), and failures are not cached (570-575). The message conflates "not installed" with "failed to start" (594), and stderr is discarded (130).
11. **Shutdown.** No wait and no SIGKILL escalation (478-488), and the reference is dropped at once (485). A server that ignores SIGTERM, or its children (tsserver, cargo, proc-macro servers), can survive (inferred for children). The `shutdown` request's 8 s timer is not unref'd.
12. **Unbounded state.** `opened` holds the full text of every file ever touched (102, 370) and `diagnosticsMap` grows with every published URI. There is no file-size cap (363).
13. **No cancellation.** An operator interrupt cannot abort a wait, and no `$/cancelRequest` is sent on timeout (296-301).
14. **Shared progress state.** `progressSeen` is reset by any edit (380-381), although parallel LSP calls are allowed (`run_turn.ts:904`).
15. **Monorepos.** One root (148) and no `workspaceFolders`, so nested Cargo, Go or tsconfig projects depend on each server's own discovery.

### Security

16. **Code execution is inside the existing trust decision (verified).** A hostile repository cannot get a server started merely by the agent asking: untrusted, read-only and sandboxed sessions are refused before spawn (`cli/src/tools.ts:1010-1016`), tested in `lsp_trust.test.ts:50-105`. In a trusted workspace a server does run project code (build scripts, proc macros, tsserver plugins, the workspace's own `typescript`) with no sandbox, the user's `HOME`, and no prompt in auto mode.
17. **Env override widens trust.** `NEXUS_TRUST_WORKSPACE=1` trusts any workspace (`cli/src/workspace_trust.ts:38`).
18. **Hover text is an unfenced injection surface.** It comes from doc comments in the workspace (`cli/src/tools.ts:1613-1617`), unlike diagnostics.
19. **Sandbox means no LSP at all.** A claim directory named `SUITE_VR1C_DEFAULT_SANDBOX_20261122` exists. If a default sandbox lands, LSP becomes unavailable by default (inferred from the name only).

### Usability

20. No configuration, no doctor finding, no manual section; the tool descriptions do not name the supported languages.
21. `docs/LSP_REAL_SERVERS.md` contradicts itself. The "Skip versus fail" section says the workflow requires `typescript,python`. "What it does not cover" says there is no incremental-edit or crash scenario and that gopls is `@latest`. Later paragraphs, the test and the workflow say the opposite.

**LSP and the type-check gate.** They are fully separate today. - LSP is per file, single root, and reads in-memory buffers (defect 1).
- The server's bundled or workspace TypeScript may differ from the project's `tsc`.
- pyright against mypy.
- `go vet` covers analyzers that gopls runs differently.
- rust-analyzer's native diagnostics against rustc's.
- LSP has timing heuristics; the gate does not.

Recommendation: LSP never satisfies or blocks the gate. It may be a clearly labelled, advisory pre-check (enhancement 6), and receipts may cite LSP records as tool facts but never as the verdict.

content.text:
The LSP review is back, and I've started the first piece of work on it: tests that pin how the language-server client behaves today, with no product change yet.

## What the review found
The security side is already strong. A language server is never started for an untrusted, read-only or sandboxed session, and its environment is scrubbed more tightly than commands' are. The weaknesses are in what the model is told, all found by reading the code and not yet confirmed by running it:

- **Stale answers reported as good.** Once a file has been opened through LSP, the server keeps its old text after the agent edits it on disk. Diagnostics or hover for another file that depends on it are then computed against the old content and reported as fine.
- **Old diagnostics returned as current** when a server published them before the file was first opened.
- **Rust times out on first use.** The tool waits 5 seconds, the client's own settling logic needs 8, and the docs record 13 to 18 seconds for a first Rust call.
- **Column positions are undefined** on any line with non-ASCII text before the symbol.
- **Hover text reaches the model unfenced**, unlike diagnostics, although it comes from doc comments in the repository.
- **Lifecycle gaps:** a missing server costs the full timeout on every call with no clear message, and shutdown doesn't wait or escalate, so a stubborn server can survive.
- **Nothing around it:** no configuration, no `nexus doctor` finding, three lines in the manual.

## Proposed scope
| Unit | What |
|---|---|
| LS-1 | Hardening: fix the defects above. |
| LS-2 | Correct positions for non-ASCII text, and nested projects in a monorepo. |
| LS-3 | First enhancements, behind an experimental setting: find-references, document and workspace symbols, warm-up so first calls don't fail, doctor findings, user-level server configuration. |
| LS-4 | More languages (clangd first), and diagnostics after an edit as an advisory signal. |

## Decisions that are yours
My defaults, until you say otherwise:
- **In v1.3.0:** LS-1, LS-2 and LS-3. LS-4 is a stretch.
- **Rename and quick fixes:** out for v1.3.0. They let a server propose file changes or run commands, so if they're ever added it should only be as proposed edits through normal approval.
- **Untrusted workspaces:** still no language server.
- **Under a sandbox:** still refused. If confinement becomes a default elsewhere, LSP would be unavailable by default, so this needs revisiting then.
- **LSP stays advisory.** The type-check gate remains the authority, and an LSP result never satisfies or blocks verification.
- **No auto-download of servers.**

## Running now
- **LS-1, slice 1:** a scripted fake language server and tests that pin current behaviour for each suspected defect. That makes each claim above confirmed or refuted by running code, and each later fix provable.
- **GV-1, slice 1:** the managed-policy library, still with its subagent.

The plan is saved at `/home/mike/nexus-wt/_plans/LSP_PLAN.md`.

<pasted_content id="2d81">

1. Core Navigation & Symbol Lookup

• Exact definitions and references: Jump straight to symbol definitions and list all usages across files instead of guessing with regex or text search.
• Document and workspace symbols: Outline file structures or search symbols across a project without reading entire files into context.
• Type and call hierarchy inspection: Read exact types, signatures, documentation, and caller/callee relationships to gauge blast radius before editing.

2. Real-Time Feedback & Self-Correction

• Incremental diagnostics: Receive type and syntax errors immediately after edits so the agent can self-correct without waiting for full builds or test runs.
• Document synchronization: Keep the language server's in-memory state aligned with the agent's edits via proper initialization, change tracking, and clean shutdown.

3. Semantic Refactoring & Editing

• Safe symbol renames: Rename functions, classes, variables, files, or folders consistently across the codebase.
• Code transformations: Support structured edits such as extracting code blocks into functions or moving functions between files.

4. Production Lifecycle & Agent Ergonomics

• Process & capability management: Handle server startup, capability discovery, workspace initialization, error recovery, and restarts reliably across languages (such as Pyright, rust-analyzer, gopls, clangd, and jdtls).
• Resource & prompt discipline: Manage cold-start indexing times and memory overhead, while guiding the agent to prefer LSP for semantic queries and grep/read for text, comments, or literals.

The managed-policy library is open as PR #717 and in CI. It is a library only: nothing in `nexus` reads a policy yet, and the docs say so at the top.

## What it contains
- **A strict parser** for a subset of TOML, which refuses anything it doesn't fully understand and gives the line number.
- **One restrict-only schema** for the system, user and project tiers. No key can grant anything.
- **A merge where the most restrictive value wins** for every key. Tier order therefore only decides which tier gets named beside a decision, and deleting a lower file can't drop below a higher one.
- **A loader that fails closed** for the system and user files, with errors naming the tier, file and line.
- **Content-hash integrity for the project file**, so its relaxations apply only after trust and only while the content matches what was approved.

I reran it after merging the current release branch: 328 tests across five files pass. The largest are a 1,449-row precedence table checked against an independently written oracle, and a 10,980-case check that a project policy can't loosen a system policy. The subagent's seven deliberate mutations were each caught.

## Where the subagent departed from the plan
I agree with all three:
- **Project relaxations are void when an administrator sets any verification key**, not only the mode. Otherwise a trusted project could exempt a path the administrator had protected.
- **The project's existing blocked-command patterns were not converted to the new rule format.** They match differently today, and converting them would have silently stopped some from matching.
- **A project file that can't be read safely** gets its own status and is not reported as removed.

## Two decisions for you before enforcement
- **A broken `/etc/nexus` directory blocks start-up even with no policy file in it.** That includes a directory that isn't root-owned or is writable by others. It's the strict reading and the safer one, but it widens what can lock an operator out.
- **The refusal messages for strict mode** were written in this slice, for example "`--yes` is refused: managed policy disables it." They're listed in `docs/MANAGED_POLICY.md` and should be agreed before a later slice prints them.

The LSP characterisation tests are still with their subagent. A watch is on #717, and it alerts me if the PR's head changes.

The LSP characterisation tests are open as PR #718, and the first fix slice is already under way.

## What running the code showed
Every defect the review predicted is real. One is worse than predicted, and two more turned up.

- **Stale answers, confirmed.** After a file changes on disk, the server keeps its old text. A go-to-definition in another file returned success pointing at line 0 for a symbol that had moved to line 3.
- **A false "clean", which is the worse one.** With the default 5-second wait and a server still analysing, the diagnostics tool returns success with no errors. I had expected "unavailable". The real error only appears on the next call.
- **Wrong symbol on non-ASCII lines, confirmed.** On a line containing `é日😀` before the symbol, the same intended position resolves to nothing, the right symbol or the wrong symbol, depending on how the model counted columns.
- **Hover is unprotected.** A 300,000-character hover containing the product's own "end of untrusted output" marker reached the model byte for byte. Nothing caps or fences it at any layer.
- **Missing server.** Five seconds on every call, with a message that can't tell "not installed" from "crashed". A server that exits with a reason on stderr loses that reason.
- **Shutdown.** A server that ignores the shutdown request stays alive, and a child process started by a well-behaved server survives it.
- **New: no input validation.** A missing line number reaches the server as `null`.
- **New: one valid definition reply shape is dropped.** A single-link reply is turned into an empty failure.

The PR adds 22 tests that pin today's behaviour, each paired with a to-do stating the target. Each later fix therefore has to flip a failing expectation, which makes it provable.

## Running now
- **LS-1 slice 2, freshness.** Before any query, every open document must match the file on disk. A diagnostics list counts only if it was published after the latest change. Documents are matched by real path, so symlinked workspaces work. When freshness can't be established in time, the answer must be "unavailable", never an old result reported as success.

input.message:
Good slice, and thank you for raising point 1 yourself: it decides whether this is usable. If rust-analyzer, gopls and pyright do not republish an unchanged list, then after every edit a diagnostics query for any OTHER open file waits the full timeout and ends unavailable. That is honest but it would make the tool useless exactly when the agent needs it (right after an edit). Fix it in this slice, in this order of preference, keeping the honesty rule (unknown is reported as unknown, never a success from old data).

## 1. Pull diagnostics where the server offers them (deterministic, preferred)
When the server's `initialize` result advertises `diagnosticProvider`, and the client has declared `textDocument.diagnostic` in its capabilities, answer a diagnostics query with a `textDocument/diagnostic` request for the queried document AFTER the sync, instead of waiting for a publish. The reply is computed for the content the server holds now, so freshness is established by construction.
- Handle the full report (`kind: "full"`, `items`) and the unchanged report (`kind: "unchanged"`, `resultId`): keep the last full list per document with its `resultId` and send `previousResultId`; an "unchanged" reply means the kept list is current. Handle `relatedDocuments` by ignoring them for the answer (do not let them overwrite other documents' state without a version check). Handle the server answering with an error or `ServerCancelled` with `retriggerRequest` (retry within the existing timeout, bounded), and a server that advertises the provider but never answers (the existing timeout, then unavailable).
- `workspace/diagnostic/refresh` from the server: answer it and treat it as "lists are no longer current".
- Read `interFileDependencies` and `workspaceDiagnostics` from the provider options and record them; do not use workspace diagnostics in this slice.
- Use the same request for the "A after B changed" case: no waiting for a republish is needed at all when pull is available.
- Declare the capability honestly in `initialize` (`textDocument.diagnostic: { dynamicRegistration: false, relatedDocumentSupport: false }`) and nothing you do not implement.

## 2. Push-only servers: accept settle EVIDENCE, not silence
For a server without `diagnosticProvider`, a list for A that predates a change to B may be returned as current only when there is positive evidence the server has processed that change:
- for a server the client already treats with `awaitProgress` (progress reporting): a work-done progress cycle that BEGAN after the change has ENDED, and the existing quiet rule holds; or
- for other servers: the server has published a list for EVERY document whose content the client changed since A's list arrived (that publish is the evidence it re-analysed), and a quiet window has passed since the last publish for any document with no publish for A. Make the quiet window a named constant with a comment saying what it trades (start with something short such as 500 ms to 1 s; justify the number), and count it from the last publish, not from the query's start.
- If neither kind of evidence arrives within the existing timeout: unavailable, with the "after another open file changed" reason you already wrote. Never a success.
- State in a comment and in the report exactly what this still gets wrong (a server that publishes for B, goes quiet for longer than the window, and only then publishes a different list for A returns A's old list as current once): that residual is why pull is preferred, and the test names should say which path they exercise.
- Your points 2 and 3 (the close-then-reopen race without versions; an in-flight versionless publish computed for old content): with pull available they do not arise for diagnostics. For push-only servers, close what you cheaply can: after a `didClose` for eviction, ignore publishes for that document until it is reopened AND a publish arrives after the reopen's `didOpen` was written, and require, for a push-only server that has EVER sent a `version` for a document, that later lists for that document carry the current version (a server that versions its publishes keeps doing so; a server that never sent a version is still answered by arrival order). Say what remains open.

## 3. Hover and definition

Two things happened: the managed-policy PR needed a conflict fix, and the LSP freshness slice came back with a problem I've sent it back to solve.

## Managed policy (#717)
- **A slip of mine, corrected.** Its checks passed, but the merge was refused because the release branch had moved and both changes appended to the same protocol README. I had written "merged" to the shared log before reading the result. I corrected the log entry straight away.
- **Now:** I merged the release branch in, kept both README sections, and re-ran its 328 tests and the schema checks, all passing. Its CI is running again.

## LSP freshness (LS-1 slice 2)
The slice fixes the stale-answer defects as designed:
- Every open document is brought in line with disk before any query.
- A diagnostics list counts only if it arrived after the latest change.
- Documents are matched by real path.
- At most 32 documents stay open.

Eleven new tests and five deliberate mutations support it.

**The problem, which the subagent raised itself:** real language servers often don't re-send a diagnostics list that hasn't changed. With the strict rule I specified, after any edit a diagnostics query for any other open file would wait the full timeout and return "unavailable". That is honest, but it would make the tool useless at the moment the agent most needs it.

**What I've asked for, in order of preference:**
- **Ask the server directly where it supports that.** Modern servers can be asked for a file's diagnostics on demand, and the answer is computed from the content the server holds right then. That makes freshness certain, with no waiting for a re-send.
- **For servers that only push, accept positive evidence, not silence.** An old list counts as current only if the server has shown it processed the change: it republished for the file that changed and then went quiet, or it finished a progress cycle that began after the change. Otherwise the answer stays "unavailable".

This can't be checked against real servers on this machine, where none is usable. The weekly real-server job is the only real validation, so I'll run it by hand before this work is called done.

<result>Pull diagnostics, settle evidence for push-only servers, and the log-barrier change are in, uncommitted, in the same five files (`tools.ts` untouched). Every requested mutation is caught and all listed suites pass; no real server ran on this host, so none of this is verified against rust-analyzer, gopls or pyright.

## Freshness rules

| Server | A diagnostics list for file A is returned as current when | Otherwise |
|---|---|---|
| Offers `diagnosticProvider` and is not staged | The reply to a `textDocument/diagnostic` request sent after the sync is a full report, or "unchanged" for a list the client kept under the `resultId` it sent. Published lists are never consulted. | Unavailable: error reply, cancellation without `retriggerRequest`, more than 3 re-asks, no reply within the call's timeout, or "unchanged" for a list not held |
| Push-only, list arrived after the latest change | At once (version must match where the server sends one) | — |
| Push-only, list predates a change to another open file | The server has published for every document changed since that list arrived, and has published nothing for `PUBLISH_QUIET_MS` | Unavailable at the timeout ("…after another open file changed") |
| Push-only, the change was a deleted file, or a changed file evicted before the server published for it | Only a new publish for A | Unavailable at the timeout |
| Staged (`awaitProgress`) | A progress cycle that began after the latest change has ended, nothing is in progress, and progress has been quiet for the existing 1500 ms | Unavailable at the timeout |

- **Pull details:** `relatedDocuments` are ignored. `workspace/diagnostic/refresh` is answered and drops every kept list, so the next request asks for a full report. `interFileDependencies` and `workspaceDiagnostics` are recorded on `client.diagnosticProvider` and not used.
- **Declared in `initialize`:** `textDocument.diagnostic: {dynamicRegistration: false, relatedDocumentSupport: false}` and `workspace.diagnostics.refreshSupport: true`.
- **Eviction:** a publish for a closed document is dropped, so a list sent between an eviction `didClose` and the reopen is never the reopened file's answer.
- **Versions:** once a server has attached a version to a list for an open document, a list without one is dropped.
- **Hover and definition:** no wait added. Right after B changed, hover on A returned B's new text in one round trip (asserted under 500 ms).

## Quiet window
`PUBLISH_QUIET_MS = 1000`, counted from the server's last publish for any file. It must outlast the gap between a server's publish for the changed file and its publish for a dependent one. I believe servers batch those within a few hundred milliseconds, but that is from memory, not measured. The cost is at most 1 s once per edit; the next query does not wait again.

## What is still wrong
- **Push-only, slow dependent:** a server that publishes for B, is silent for more than 1 s, and only then publishes a different list for A has A's old list returned as current once. This is the `KNOWN LIMIT (push)` test.
- **Push-only, no versions, clear after reopen:** an empty "clear" list sent for a close that arrives after the reopen's `didOpen` was written is still accepted. Only the window before the reopen is closed.
- **Push-only, no versions, in-flight list:** a list computed for old content that arrives after the `didChange` was written is still accepted.
- **Staged servers:** "began after the change" is judged by when the begin message arrived, so a cycle the server started just before reading the change can count.
- **Deleted file on a push-only server:** A stays unavailable until the server publishes for A again.

## Decisions for you
- **Staged servers get no pull.** For `awaitProgress` servers (rust-analyzer in the built-in table) I do not declare the capability or use pull. I recall rust-analyzer's pull returning only its native diagnostics while cargo-check results still arrive by publish, so pulling could lose errors. Unverified. The catch is that Rust keeps the weaker progress rule; say if you want pull there too.
- **Version flag scope.** The flag is set only by a versioned list for an open document, not by one for an unopened file. A server that mixes versioned and unversioned lists for open documents would lose the unversioned ones.
- **New unavailable reason.** Pull failures read "Language server 'X' gave no diagnostics for F: <why>". The tool wrapper is unchanged.

## Existing tests changed
- `CURRENT (defects 4, 15)` now expects the two new capability entries in `initialize`.
- `FIXED (defect 2)`: c.ts's post-open list now carries a version, because that fake attaches versions to b.ts's lists and the new rule would drop an unversioned one. The version-less server case is in the freshness file.

The LSP freshness slice is done and pushed, and the next LSP slice is already being built.

## Freshness slice (LS-1 slice 2), as reviewed
I reran it after merging in the latest branches: 23 characterisation tests, 22 freshness tests and the four existing LSP suites pass, with no process left behind.

- **Every open document is brought in line with disk before any query.** A hover right after another file changed now returns the answer from the new text in one round trip.
- **Diagnostics are asked for directly** where the server supports that, so the answer is computed from current content with no waiting.
- **Servers that only push** have an old list accepted only with evidence they processed the change: they republished for the changed file and then stayed quiet for one second. Otherwise the answer is "unavailable".
- **At most 32 documents stay open.** The least recently used is closed.
- **Symlinked workspaces work**, because documents are matched by real path.

Its PR opens once #718 merges.

## What it doesn't solve, each pinned as a named "known limit" test
- A push-only server that republishes for the changed file, stays silent for over a second, and only then sends a different list for a dependent file gets its old list accepted once.
- Rust keeps the weaker progress-based rule. The subagent recalled that rust-analyzer's direct-ask path omits cargo-check errors, so it didn't use that path there. That recollection is unverified.
- **None of this has been run against a real language server.** No usable server exists on this machine. The weekly real-server workflow is the only real check, and I'll run it by hand on this branch before calling the unit done.

## Running now
- **LS-1 slice 3: timeouts, readiness and start failures.**

## What
LSP maturity (owner priority 6), unit LS-1, slice 2: freshness. Slice 1 (#718) measured that the language-server client answered from stale state and reported it as success. This slice removes those answers.

Changes are in `cli/src/lsp.ts` only (`cli/src/tools.ts` is untouched), plus tests. Tool names, schemas and output shapes do not change.

## What was wrong (measured in #718) and what happens now
| Before | Now |
|---|---|
| After file B changed on disk, the server kept B's old text; hover and definition on file A answered from it as a success. | Every query goes through one entry point that first brings every open document in line with the file on disk. Hover on A right after B changed returns the answer from B's new text in one round trip. |
| A diagnostics list published before a file's first open was returned as its first answer. | A list counts for a file only if it arrived after the client's latest change, and where the server sends versions, only if the version matches. |
| In a symlinked workspace, a server that publishes under the canonical URI was never matched: "published no diagnostics within 5000ms". | Documents are identified by real path; incoming URIs are decoded and compared as paths. Works with a server that canonicalises and with one that echoes. |
| Every file ever queried stayed open; no `didClose` was ever sent. | At most 32 documents stay open (`MAX_OPEN_DOCUMENTS`); the least recently queried is closed with `didClose`. A document that vanished, stopped being a regular file, or now resolves outside the workspace is closed and never read. |

## How freshness of diagnostics is established
| Server | A list for file A is returned as current when | Otherwise |
|---|---|---|
| Offers `diagnosticProvider` (and is not a staged server) | The reply to a `textDocument/diagnostic` request sent after the sync is a full report, or "unchanged" for a list the client holds under the `resultId` it sent. Published lists are not consulted. | Unavailable: an error reply, cancellation without retrigger, more than 3 re-asks, no reply in time, or "unchanged" for a list not held |
| Push-only, list arrived after the latest change | At once | |
| Push-only, list predates a change to another open file | The server has published for every document changed since, and has then been quiet for `PUBLISH_QUIET_MS` (1,000 ms) | Unavailable at the timeout, with the reason "after another open file changed" |
| Staged (`awaitProgress`: rust-analyzer in the built-in table) | A progress cycle that began after the latest change has ended and progress has been quiet for the existing 1,500 ms | Unavailable at the timeout |

Unknown is reported as unknown: when freshness cannot be established, the answer is unavailable ("This is not evidence the file is free of errors"), never an old list as a success.

Why pull where it exists: real servers often do not republish a list that did not change, so a publish-only rule would leave every other open file "unavailable" for the full timeout after each edit, exactly when the agent needs an answer.

## Change detection cost
Per open document per query: one `realpath` and one `stat` (device, inode, size, mtime and ctime in nanoseconds). A file whose newest timestamp is younger than 2 s is also read and compared by content, so a second write inside one clock tick is caught. Measured: 2 + 2n file-system calls for n settled open documents (22 at 10, 66 at 32), about 2 to 7 ms at 32 documents; a diagnostics query costs one request with pull.

## Known limits, each a test named `KNOWN LIMIT` or stated here
- **Not verified against real servers.** No usable language server exists on the development host. The weekly `lsp-real-servers` workflow is the real check; it should be run by hand on this branch before LS-1 is called done.
- Push-only, slow dependent: a server that publishes for B, stays silent for more than 1 s, and only then publishes a different list for A has A's old list returned as current once.
- Push-only without versions: a list computed for old content that arrives after the `didChange` was written is still accepted; an empty "clear" sent for a close that arrives after the reopen is still accepted.
- Staged servers get no pull. The author recalls rust-analyzer's pull returning only its native diagnostics while cargo-check results arrive by publish, so pulling could lose errors; this is unverified, and it means Rust keeps the weaker progress rule.
- "Began after the change" for a progress cycle is judged by when the begin message arrived.
- A file changed on disk that was never opened through LSP is left to the server's own watcher.
- Missed change detection: a writer through `mmap` on an already dirty page, a file system that does not maintain ctime, a clock stepped back more than 2 s.

## Tests
- `lsp_characterization`: the `CURRENT` tests for defects 1, 2, 6 and the unbounded open set are replaced by `FIXED` tests; each `CURRENT` test was confirmed failing against the fix first. 23 pass, 18 todo remain for later slices.
- New `lsp_freshness`: 22 tests (deleted and renamed files; a file or its directory replaced by a link leaving the workspace, with a spy showing no read; parallel queries with an edit between; servers with and without versions; six pull cases; six push cases including the known limit; eviction; paths with spaces and non-ASCII characters).
- The harness's log readers are now asynchronous and do a round trip first, so a log is never read before the fake wrote it (the race that failed #718 once on Node 22).
- Mutations, each caught and restored: no re-sync of other documents; an old list counted as current; raw string URI compare; no `didClose` on eviction; a cached list returned as success when freshness is not established; ignoring `diagnosticProvider`; "unchanged" without a held list read as clean; silence accepted as settle evidence; a progress cycle begun before the change counted; a publish between eviction and reopen counted.
- After merging the release branch: `lsp_characterization` 23, `lsp_freshness` 22, `lsp_honesty` 13, `lsp_progress` 4, `lsp_trust` 14 pass; before it also `cg3_diagnostics_evidence` 13 and `lsp_real_servers` (2 pass, 12 skipped for lack of servers). `tsc` clean, leak check clean, no surviving process. Node 24 locally; CI covers Node 22.

## Next
Slice 3: timeouts, readiness and start failures (the false clean while a server is still analysing, "nothing here" versus "not ready", a missing server). Slice 4: lifecycle and bounds. Slice 5: output.

No `CHANGELOG.md` entry (claimed by another lane; collected at release preparation).

The local XERJ node was queried twice (opencode corpus, index flagged not verified complete) for LSP client synchronisation; only the LSP documentation page came back, no client code. Nothing taken or copied. The young-timestamp rule follows the well-known racy-timestamp idea in git's index.

### Shutdown sequence
`LspClient.shutdown()` and `LspBridgeManager.shutdownAll()` return a promise that never rejects; a second call returns the same stop.

| Step | Wait | Constant |
|---|---|---|
| `shutdown` request, wait for reply or exit | 2 s | `LSP_SHUTDOWN_REPLY_MS` |
| `exit` notification, wait for exit | 1 s | `LSP_EXIT_GRACE_MS` |
| SIGTERM to the process group | 2 s | `LSP_TERM_GRACE_MS` |
| SIGKILL to the group and the child | 1 s (only bounds an unkillable process) | `LSP_KILL_GRACE_MS` |

- **Why these numbers:** all four are judgements, and the code comment says so. `docs/LSP_REAL_SERVERS.md` records no shutdown timing. A server that ignores everything is gone 5 s after the call.
- **After exit:** the client waits for the stderr drain and destroys the pipes, so no timer or handle is left.
- **Not yet initialised, or failed:** killed at once, no protocol steps.
- **Process group:** servers are spawned `detached` on POSIX, not unref'd. The group is also swept with SIGKILL the moment the server exits, however it ended (crash included).
- **Server that left its group:** signalling falls back to the child itself.
- **Grandchild in its own session:** out of reach and not waited for (tested: shutdown does not hang or throw).
- **Windows:** no groups, child only, untested.
- **Process exit:** the `process.on("exit")` hook now SIGKILLs every live group (running, starting, or mid-stop). Tested with a real child process that calls `process.exit` without shutting down.
- **In-flight queries:** end at once with `Language server '<cmd>' was stopped.`
- **Gate refusal:** now also stops a server that is still starting.

### Server requests and answers

| Request | Answer |
|---|---|
| `workspace/applyEdit` | `{applied: false, failureReason: "This client does not let a language server edit files."}` |
| `workspace/configuration` | one `null` per item; `[]` with no items; more than 256 items gets `-32602` |
| `client/registerCapability` | `null`; id and method recorded (`LspClient.registrations()`), at most 256, oldest dropped |
| `client/unregisterCapability` | `null`; removed (accepts the protocol's `unregisterations` spelling) |
| `window/workDoneProgress/create` | `null` |
| `window/showMessageRequest` | `null` |
| `workspace/workspaceFolders` | `[{uri: <rootUri>, name: <basename>}]` |
| `workspace/diagnostic/refresh` | `null`, S2 behaviour kept |
| anything else | error `-32601`, `Method not found: <method>` |

### Caps

| Cap | Value | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| `LSP_MAX_FILE_BYTES` | 2 MiB | imported from `file_diff.ts` `MAX_SNAPSHOT_BYTES` (the edit path's "too large for line detail" limit) |
| `LSP_MAX_MESSAGE_BYTES` | 16 MiB | the existing limit, pinned by `lsp_trust` |
| header block | 8 KiB | bytes that never form a header are not collected past this |
| `LSP_MAX_DIAGNOSTICS` | 50 | equals `MAX_DIAGNOSTIC_RECORDS`, so the fence never truncates a second time |
| diagnostic message / source and code | 1000 / 200 chars | bounds what the client retains |
| pull `resultId` | 1024 chars | longer is not kept; the next request asks for a full report |
| `LSP_MAX_DEFINITION_TARGETS` | 20 | judgement |
| `LSP_MAX_HOVER_CHARS` | 8000 | judgement |
| progress tokens / registrations / message ring | 256 / 256 / 20 | judgement |

- **File cap:** checked by `fstat` on the open descriptor before any read; measured in bytes. A file that grows past it while open is closed without a read, and asking for it gives the refusal.
- **Message cap:** refused on the announced `Content-Length`; the client then reads nothing more, kills the group, and records failure kind `message_too_large`. Restarts are paced and capped like a crash.
- **Diagnostics over 50:** the most severe are kept first, and one line follows the fence: `+N more, less severe or later in the server's list`.
- **File and message caps are injectable** through a new `limits` option beside `timings`.

**Worst-case retained memory** (comment in `lsp.ts`):
`MAX_OPEN_DOCUMENTS × (2×fileBytes + 2×50×2×(1000+2×200) + 2×1024) + messageBytes + 8 KiB + one 64 KiB chunk + 4 KiB stderr + 256×400 + 256×800 + 20×2×560`.

content.text:
LSP slices 4 and 5 are reviewed, committed and pushed, and the first run against real language servers is now in progress on that branch.

## What slices 4 and 5 do
- **Shutdown ends the process for certain.** It escalates from a shutdown request to a forced kill within about 5 s, and anything the server started dies with it. A sweep at exit covers a Nexus that quit without shutting down.
- **Server requests get correct answers.** A server asking to edit files is refused; unknown requests get a proper error, where they used to get a fake success.
- **Bounds.**
  - Files over 2 MiB are refused before being read.
  - A server message over 16 MiB fails the server.
  - Diagnostics are capped at 50, most severe first, with a count of the rest.
- **Inputs are validated.** Line and character must be positive integers, and the file must exist inside the workspace before any server starts.
- **One definition shape.** Every answer form becomes a workspace-relative file with 1-based positions, so an answer can be passed straight back as a question.
- **Hover is treated as untrusted text.** It is sanitised, redacted, capped at 8,000 characters and fenced, as diagnostics already are.

The subagent reported all 13 deliberate mutations caught. After my change, 36 concurrent runs of the nine LSP suites had no failures.

## One judgement I changed in review
A diagnostic that arrives with no severity is now reported as an **error**, not "information". The reader is an agent deciding whether its edit broke something, so an unlabelled real error must not read as a remark.

## Things you may want to know
- **Tool descriptions grew** from 1,339 to 1,855 characters across the three LSP tools. That costs prompt tokens on every turn where they are loaded.
- **Servers now run in their own process group.** Ctrl-C no longer reaches them directly; Nexus stops them itself. If Nexus is force-killed, they exit only when their input closes.
- **Worst-case memory held by the client** is about 153 MiB, reached with 32 open files each at the 2 MiB limit.
- **The manual still quotes the old hover description.** That is for the docs slice.

## Real-server validation
I dispatched the real-server workflow on the branch carrying slices 2 to 5 (run 45051117528). It is the first check of any of this against the pinned real servers. I'll read its result before merging slices 3 to 5.

## Still running
- CI on the release branch after the audit test fix, and on #733.
- The managed-policy enforcement subagent.

Produce an implementation plan for unit AC-1 of the nexus-code v1.3.0 plan: an ACP (Agent Client Protocol) adapter that lets an ACP host (an editor or another harness) drive Nexus over stdio. This is READ-ONLY planning: do not edit, create or delete any file in the repository, do not commit, push or run `gh`. Your only output is the plan in your final message (I will save it). Repository: read from the git worktree `/home/mike/nexus-wt/ls1b` (a checkout of the release branch line; do not modify it) or use `git -C /home/mike/nexus-code show origin/release/v1.3.0:<path>` for the exact release-branch content.

## Read first
1. `AGENTS.md` (repository root).
2. `docs/v1.3.0/PLAN.md` on `origin/release/v1.3.0`: the theme, the security principles (numbered list near the top), unit rows AC-1 and AC-2 and the paragraph after them (it supersedes v1.2.1 unit RD-5), VR-2, PF-1 to PF-4, gates G-2 and G-3, decisions D13 and D14 with their defaults, and the phase list.
3. What already exists for PF-1 and PF-2 on the release branch: `docs/protocol/` (README, `sidecar-v1.schema.json`, `VERSIONS.json`, the run-result and verify-result schemas), `cli/src/protocol.ts`, `cli/src/sidecar.ts` (the NDJSON sidecar the Rust TUI drives: message kinds, `hello`/`initialize` and capability negotiation, how a turn is started and cancelled, how approvals are requested and answered, how tool calls, diffs, verification results and receipts are emitted, how sessions are created, saved and resumed), `cli/src/run_contract.ts`, the wire fixtures and conformance tests for the protocol (search `cli/test` for `protocol`, `sidecar`, `wire`, `conformance`), and how `serve-mcp` is implemented and tested (it is the existing precedent for "Nexus as a stdio server for another program": find its command registration, its JSON-RPC framing code and its tests, and whether its framing can be shared).
4. The approval and gate path a tool call takes (`cli/src/core/dispatch_tool_call.ts`, `cli/src/core/approval_policy.ts`, the sidecar's approval handling including its "always approve" flag) so the plan can state exactly where an ACP permission reply enters and why an `allow` reply cannot override a gate that denies.
5. The ACP specification as far as you can establish it WITHOUT guessing. Sources, in order: (a) the local XERJ reference node, which indexes peer projects that implement ACP servers and clients: read `docs/XERJ_REFERENCE_CODING.md` for the commands and corpora, then query for the ACP method names and shapes (`initialize`, `session/new`, `session/load`, `session/prompt`, `session/cancel`, `session/update`, `session/request_permission`, `tool_call`, `tool_call_update`, protocol version, content blocks, stop reasons, `fs/read_text_file`, `fs/write_text_file`, `terminal/*`, `authenticate`, extension methods and the underscore prefix rule, `_meta`); record file and line for each fact; (b) any ACP schema, SDK types or docs vendored in those corpora or present on this host (`find` under `~` for `agent-client-protocol`, `acp` schema json, with care not to read secrets or anything under `~/.nexus` or `~/.config/nexus/config.env`); (c) no network access is available to you. For every protocol fact in your plan say which source it came from, and list separately every fact you could NOT verify locally and that the implementer must check against the published specification before relying on it. Do not present a recalled detail as verified.

## What the plan must contain
1. **Facts about today's code**, with file and line pointers: the sidecar's message flow for one turn end to end, what a session is and how it is resumed, how approvals work, what receipts and verification results look like on the wire, and what `serve-mcp` shares.
2. **Architecture decision** with the alternatives considered: (A) a new `nexus acp` command that runs an in-process adapter on top of the same agent/session objects the sidecar uses; (B) an adapter process that spawns the sidecar and translates NDJSON to ACP JSON-RPC (the plan row says "over the sidecar protocol"); (C) something else. Recommend one, on the grounds of: one enforcement path for gates and approvals (no second path that can drift), testability without a model, the published sidecar schema as the contract, startup cost, and how much existing code must be edited. State what the choice means for PF-4 (library entry) and VR-2.
3. **Method-by-method mapping table**: every ACP method and notification Nexus will implement in v1.3.0, the sidecar message(s) it maps to and from, the fields, and what is deliberately NOT implemented (and how that is declared in the capability list so a client does not call it). Include: protocol-version negotiation and what happens on a mismatch; `session/new` (cwd, MCP server list: whether client-supplied MCP servers are accepted at all, given the managed-policy MCP allowlist of unit GV-5 and the workspace-trust rules: recommend refusing or ignoring them in v1.3.0 and say how that is reported); `session/load` replay; `session/prompt` content blocks accepted (text; resource links; images or audio: refuse); streaming updates (agent message chunks, thought chunks if any, plan updates, `tool_call`, `tool_call_update` with diff content); stop reasons including cancellation and refusal; `session/cancel` semantics and the race with an in-flight permission request; the `verification` update carrying receipt ids and verifier results (how it is carried: a standard update kind if one fits, otherwise an extension notification, named per the specification's extension rule); `_nexus/receipt/get`; client-side file system and terminal capabilities (recommend NOT using the client's `fs/*` or `terminal/*` in v1.3.0 so that every read, write and command stays inside Nexus's own gates and sandbox; say what that costs, for example unsaved editor buffers are not seen).
4. **Permission model**, the security core. `session/request_permission` offers allow-once and reject only. State precisely: which Nexus decisions are surfaced as a permission request and which are never asked (a gate that denies is final: managed policy, read-only mode, verification-file protection, command rules, sandbox, workspace trust); that the reply is treated as an operator answer only for a call that is pending approval, bound to that call's id and content (a reply for an unknown, stale, already-answered or different call is ignored and logged; replay and reordering cases); what the default is when the client never answers, disconnects or cancels (deny); that no reply can change the approval mode ("allow always" is not offered, and an option id the adapter did not offer is treated as reject); how the session's approval mode and workspace trust are established at start (the ACP client cannot grant trust or select full access through the protocol; they come from the operator's own configuration, flags and managed policy on the machine where Nexus runs); and what an untrusted workspace or a broken managed policy looks like to an ACP client (a clear error at `initialize` or `session/new`, never a silent downgrade). Treat every string from the client as untrusted input: size limits per message and per field, depth limits, a bound on concurrent sessions and pending requests, path validation for `cwd` (must exist, be a directory, be canonicalised; what about a cwd outside any trusted workspace), and no client string reaching a shell, a file path or the model unfenced where fencing is the existing rule.
5. **Framing and robustness**: the JSON-RPC 2.0 framing ACP uses over stdio as verified from the sources (newline-delimited or Content-Length: establish which, do not assume), request/response correlation, errors and codes, batch requests (refuse), notifications, malformed input, oversized lines, stdout hygiene (nothing but protocol on stdout: where existing code prints to stdout and how that is redirected), EOF and signals (the adapter and any child it started exit; no orphan), backpressure on streaming.
6. **Test strategy** with no model and no network: a scripted ACP client test harness and a scripted model/gateway (find how existing tests fake the gateway, for example a local scripted gateway helper, and reuse it); the acceptance tests of the plan row ("a scripted ACP client completes a task; an `allow` reply to an action the gates deny has no effect (gate test G-3); the receipt is retrievable"); a hostile-client suite (every case in item 4, malformed and oversized frames, unknown methods, wrong session ids, cancel races, disconnect mid-turn with processes asserted gone by pid); golden wire fixtures committed under a `docs/protocol` or `cli/test/fixtures` path consistent with PF-1's fixtures, which unit AC-2 will later compare against real clients; how the adapter's own message types get a generated schema and drift test in the PF-1 pattern (types module, generator script, ledger, test). Each real-CLI child process start costs about 3 s through the TypeScript loader and 0.65 s from a current `dist` build: say how the tests stay well under 60 s per file (a test file over 300 s fails CI).
7. **Slices**: an ordered list of small PR-sized slices (each independently mergeable into `release/v1.3.0`, each with its files, its tests and its acceptance check), with slice 1 creating ONLY new files (pure types, framing, mapping functions and their tests) so it can start while other agents hold claims on existing files. For every existing file a later slice must edit (for example `cli/src/index.ts` for the command, `cli/src/sidecar.ts`, `docs/USER_MANUAL.md`, `docs/protocol/README.md`), name the file, the size of the edit and why it cannot be avoided. Note that `cli/src/index.ts`, `cli/src/agent.ts`, `cli/src/core/spine_handlers.ts`, `cli/src/sidecar.ts`, `cli/src/types.ts` and `cli/src/sandbox.ts` are held or wanted by another agent right now.
8. **What the release can honestly claim** after AC-1 without AC-2 (gate G-2 says AC-1 passes against two real clients or the release says "experimental"): the exact wording for the documentation, and the list of open risks.
9. **Decisions needed from the owner**, each with a recommended default so work is not blocked: at least the command name and whether it is hidden or marked experimental; client-supplied MCP servers; use of client `fs/*` and `terminal/*`; authentication (stdio only, none) and that no network listener is opened in this unit (PF-3 is separate); which two clients for AC-2 (D14 default).

## Constraints on you
Read-only. No network. Never read or print `~/.config/nexus/config.env` or anything under `~/.nexus`. Do not run tests that take long; reading code is enough, plus short commands (`git grep`, `git show`, `xerj ...`). Keep the final plan dense and concrete (file paths, function names, message names, numbers), with an explicit "verified from <source>" or "NOT verified locally" mark on every ACP protocol fact. Aim for a plan an implementer can follow without re-deriving anything, in roughly 250 to 400 lines.

- `cancel` (no id) aborts the turn's `AbortController` (496-507); the turn ends `INTERRUPTED`.
- Every event passes `formatSafeSidecarEvent` (1381-1397: redaction, control characters made visible, `FIELD_LIMITS` 1312-1330) and fails closed.

**Sessions**
- One `SidecarServer` owns one `ApplicationCore` (`cli/src/core/app.ts:88-102`), one workspace and one session id (`generateSessionId`, `cli/src/session.ts:119`; constructor at sidecar.ts:149).
- A session record is written after each turn and on progress (1114-1155), and not while only the system prompt exists (1117).
- Resume happens only at start (`--resume [id]`, 163-172 → `resumeSession` 1157-1178). It switches the workspace to the session's own (1167), restores the conversation, and emits `history` with the last 60 entries of 4,000 chars each (27-28, 1186-1214).
- A failed resume is only a `notice` text; there is no structured result. `resolveResumeId` (session.ts:207-230) also accepts `latest` and scans the directory.

**Approvals**
- The gate is `cli/src/core/dispatch_tool_call.ts`. Refusals that happen before any prompt:
  - delegation authority (94-117)
  - role allow and deny lists (121-148)
  - skill constraint and integrity (151-218)
  - forbidden deletion (235-258)
  - checkpoint read-only fallback (272-307)
  - verification-file protection (339-388)
  - command rule `forbidden` (415-441)
  - untrusted workspace skill (457-482)
- `askOperator` is computed at 451-455 from `ApprovalPolicy.requiresDecision` (`cli/src/core/approval_policy.ts:29-88`), a command rule `prompt`, a verification edit `ask`, an injection suspicion, or a re-issued interrupted call.
- Read-only mode never asks (approval_policy.ts:47-50). The mutating call is refused later inside `spine.execute` with `context.readOnly` (dispatch 605-608, 681), as is the sandbox.
- Only when `askOperator` is true is `onConfirm` called (553). A false answer gives a `DENIED` receipt (563-600).
- Sidecar side: `confirmFor` (727-732) → `requestApproval` (848-853, one at a time through `approvalTail`) → `openApproval` (855-879) emits `approval.request {id:"approval-N", turn_id, tool, subject, preview, review}`. An abort settles it false (861).
- `approve {id, always}` and `deny {id}` → `resolveApproval` (881-896). A wrong id gives `NO_PENDING_APPROVAL`. `always:true` sets `alwaysApprove` and switches the agent to `auto` (887-892).
- `approval.request` carries no `call_id`.
- `review` is `ApprovalReview` (`cli/src/approval_review.ts:12-17`): `change {path, before, after}`, `patch`, `command`, `verifier`, `args`.

**Receipts and verification on the wire**
- `turn.result.turn` is `TurnResult` (`cli/src/core/turn.ts:296`): `execution` (line 17), `outcome` `VERIFIED|REGRESSION_FREE|UNVERIFIED|NOT_ESTABLISHED|NOT_REQUIRED` (27), `reason`, `verification: VerificationEvidence` (193), `turnEvidence.verifierRuns` (419), `unverifiedChangesPending`.
- The `receipt {id}` command returns `receipt {sections: ReceiptSection[]}` (`cli/src/evidence.ts:153`).
- The validation receipt id appears only as the row `["receipt", receiptId]` of the section titled "Validation receipt" (evidence.ts:216-238; type `ValidationReceipt`, `cli/src/core/candidate.ts:50-63`). It exists only with `--authoritative-verifier`.

**`serve-mcp`**
- Registered at `cli/src/index.ts:1192-1201`; class `McpServer` at `cli/src/mcp.ts:912`.
- It uses an inline newline-delimited JSON-RPC loop with no line cap and no shared framing module, and a hard-coded version "1.2.1". Its tests call `handleMessage` in-process (`cli/test/harness.test.ts:222`, `:2620`).
- Nothing in it is reusable as framing; AC-1 writes its own module. `serve-mcp` could adopt that module later, which is out of scope here.

**Other facts the plan relies on**
- Managed policy is a library only. `loadManagedPolicy` (`cli/src/core/managed_policy_load.ts:374`) has no caller outside `core/managed_policy*.ts`, and `docs/protocol/README.md` ends "nexus does not read a policy file yet".
